newsitem.title: PAKISTAN: Strike called by Moslem group hits Karachi.
newsitem.headline: Strike called by Moslem group hits Karachi.

text.p: A strike called by a militant Sunni Moslem group reduced commercial activity and public transport in the southern port city of Karachi on Tuesday, witnesses said.
Police and paramilitary rangers patrolled main roads in Pakistan's biggest city and guarded commercial centres and mosques to prevent any outbreak of violence.
The strike was in response to the death of Sipah-i-Sahaba Pakistan (SSP) chief Zia-ur-Rahman Faruqi, who was among 26 people killed in the bombing at a courthouse in Lahore on Saturday.

The blast, which Sunni hardliners blame on Iran and the local Shi'ite Tehrik-i-Jafria Pakistan (TJP) group, has raised fears of sectarian unrest two weeks before Pakistani elections on February 3. The TJP has condemned the blast.
There were no immediate reports of violence or arson, but witnesses said public transport was thin and private vehicles avoided areas considered to be SSP strongholds.
Most shopping centres and wholesale markets were partly shut as some traders kept their shutters down for fear of violence.
The Karachi Stock Exchange opened for business, but then closed because of thin attendance, a bourse official said.
Bankers said most banks in the southern commercial district were open and the strike would not affect interbank trading.
"The strike has only hit public transport. I think office attendance has not been affected as much as in previous strikes," said a foreign banker, who asked not to be named.
On Sunday, SSP activists sacked and burned the Iranian cultural centre in Lahore, drawing a protest from Tehran.

"What took place in Pakistan in recent days is the result of actions by America and the Zionist regime (Israel) which are provoking sectarianism," Iranian radio quoted Iranian Deputy Foreign Minister Alaeddin Boroujerdi as saying.
"America's anti-Islamic move in Pakistan will in no way affect the level of ties between Iran and Pakistan," he said.

No group has claimed responsibility for the bomb blast. It appeared to be the latest incident in a long-running feud between militants in Pakistan's majority Sunni and minority Shi'ite communities, which cost about 170 lives last year.

Police said on Monday that a Shi'ite activist named Mehram Ali, 35, had confessed to detonating the bomb by remote control as Faruqi and his deputy, Azam Tariq, arrived at the Lahore court to face charges of involvement in sectarian murders.
Lahore's regional police chief, deputy inspector general Tariq Pervez, said Ali had told police that his main target was Tariq because of his speeches attacking Shi'ite leaders.
Shi'ites form about 15 percent of Pakistan's population of over 130 million, but are a majority in neighbouring Iran.
